contributions.headingText: Immature teratoma is a teratoma containing immature and variable amounts of mature tissues.
2C73.3 & XH0N49 Malignant teratoma of ovary & Immature teratoma, malignant

Immature teratoma usually presents as a pelvic mass {992645}. Elevated serum AFP should prompt more-extensive sampling of the tumour to rule out yolk sac tumour, but tumours with hepatoid components may have elevated AFP {30634670}.
This is the second most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumour in the USA {16648414}, usually presenting within the first three decades of life {992645}.

Immature teratomas may develop similarly to mature cystic teratoma via a common origin involving germ cells at the same developmental stage {16258281; 28664933}. They usually do not exhibit gain of 12p or isochromosome 12p unless they are part of a mixed germ cell tumour {9679978; 10850452; 16547466}.
These tumours are usually unilateral, large, fleshy, greyish-tan, and solid-cystic, with haemorrhage and necrosis {1260722}.

Variable amounts of immature tissues, mostly neuroectodermal tubules and rosettes, are admixed with ectodermal and endodermal tissues of varying maturation. The tubules and rosettes are composed of mitotically active hyperchromatic cells. Cellular, mitotically active glia may also be present. Immature mesodermal and, less commonly, endodermal tissues may be present. Immature teratoma should not have foci of yolk sac tumour. If such foci are present, the case should be classified as mixed germ cell tumour; if the patient has an apparent immature teratoma but elevated serum levels of AFP, that should prompt additional sampling of the specimen to find a focus/component of yolk sac tumour, which would change the classification to mixed germ cell tumour.

SALL4 can be positive in immature neuroectoderm and intestinal elements {19295406; 23240671}. SOX2 and glypican-3 (GPC3) can be positive in neuroectoderm. AFP may stain immature gastrointestinal-type glands. A trabecular or nested proliferation of thin-walled blood vessels may be present, mimicking a vascular neoplasm {11781518; 12068181}.

Grading (see #13059Table #13059) is based on the number of low-power microscopic fields (diameter = 4.5 mm) containing aggregated amounts of immature neuroepithelium in any one slide {1260722; 7814189}. Metastatic sites of immature teratoma are graded using the same criteria; pure gliomatosis peritonei is considered mature (grade 0).
Essential: a germ cell tumour with immature neuroectodermal tissue.

This entity is staged according to the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM classification (see TNM staging of ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal carcinoma [[Brierley JD, Gospodarowicz MK, Wittekind C, editors. TNM classification of malignant tumours. 8th ed. Oxford (UK): Wiley-Blackwell; 2017.]]) and the FIGO staging system. Although gliomatosis peritonei represents stage III disease, its behaviour is generally regarded as benign, and overtreatment should be avoided.

Stage and grade of the primary tumour and grade of the metastatic tumour (if present) are the main prognostic factors. The 5-year overall survival rate is > 90%. For stage I tumours, the 5-year survival rate approaches 100% {27423379; 21764111; 27222024; 7522313}. There is controversy as to the most appropriate way to stage immature teratoma and gliomatosis. Current evidence indicates that gliomatosis is a benign condition that does not require chemotherapy {5521737; 26564007; 22820986} and that some cases occur in patients with benign ovarian tumours or no ovarian tumours at all {10726696}. This means that implants must be adequately sampled by the surgeon and carefully and thoroughly evaluated by the pathologist. The current recommendation from UICC is that gliomatosis should be staged when associated with an ovarian immature teratoma [[Wittekind C, Brierley JD, Lee A, et al., editors. TNM supplement: a commentary on uniform use. 5th ed. Hoboken (NJ): Wiley-Blackwell; 2019.]], but there is no outcome-based evidence to support that guidance. In the absence of such evidence, many clinicians and pathologists discount the presence of pure gliomatosis and upstage the ovarian tumour only if the implants contain immature elements (i.e. grade 1 or higher). Whichever approach is taken, it is essential that the nature of the implants be carefully documented and the prognostic significance be clearly communicated to the treating clinicians. After chemotherapy, rare patients may develop extraovarian deposits of pure mature teratomatous tissue, so-called growing teratoma syndrome {27258729; 26262454; 18043048}.
